name: vessel
description: Use when working in packages/vessel, or when adding mini apps, live views, media sources, pub/sub events or GPU passes. Vessel is a toolkit of small crates for building applications.
---

Vessel is a toolkit of small crates for building applications that are easy to develop, configure, and deploy. An app is made of pieces that plug into a shared engine, so the same app can run in different places.

Code Name: Vessel

# What is an app?

In Vessel, an app is anything that shows something and reacts to changes. It can be small, like a single component (a video viewer inside a larger application), or large, like a whole mobile app or video game.

An app is built from a few simple parts:

- A **view** that shows something: a photo, a video, a game, or anything else that can draw itself.
- **Messages** that tell the view what changed, such as "brightness is now 30".
- An **engine** that decides when to draw the view. The app never says "draw now".

The goal is to write an app once and run it on many platforms and in many formats without changing its code.

## Example use cases

These are the goals. Not all of them work yet.

- A component
  - A video viewer is developed once, then shown inside an existing application.
  - An image renderer is developed once, then shown inside an existing application.
  - A custom button component.
- An application
  - A video game that renders an entire window.
  - A desktop application, such as an image editor.
  - A mobile app/game.

Today, the only app using Vessel is the mobile app (`packages/react-native/alakazam`). It runs on Android, and so far only for a live photo preview with a brightness slider. The desktop app is on hold, and video sources are not built yet.

# Where things live

Vessel is a set of small crates in `packages/vessel`. They do not depend on abra, so each one can be published on its own. Names may change later, so check each folder's `Cargo.toml` for the current package name.

- `packages/vessel/events`: the pub/sub event system (`Subject`, `BehaviorSubject`, and the `Observable` and `Observer` traits) with the operators `filter`, `map`, `filter_map`, `scan` (returns a `BehaviorSubject` of the running state), `merge`, `distinct_until_changed`, `combine_latest` and `take_until`. The package is currently `pub-sub`.
- `packages/vessel/vessel` (package `vessel`): **the one crate an app depends on.** It re-exports the engine, the API and the controls, and `use vessel::prelude::*;` is the one import for the whole toolkit (also `vessel::engine`, `vessel::api`, `vessel::ui` by name). Features `desktop-window` and `android-surface` are set here. Nothing else should depend on the parts directly except other Vessel crates.
- `packages/vessel/engine` (package `vessel-engine`): the view engine (`Engine`, `View`, `Frame`, `MediaSource`, `Waker`, and `GpuFrame`/`GpuTarget` for pictures that live on the GPU). It decides when to draw and knows nothing about components.
- `packages/vessel/api` (package `vessel-api`): the API that apps are written against. Built so far: `Component` (typed events, `watch`, `draw`, and it is a `MediaSource`), `BehaviorSubject<T>`, a small `Canvas`, the neutral input events (`KeyEvent`, `PointerEvent`, `Quit`), `AppOptions`, `App`, CSS-like layout, `run` with the desktop window host (flag `desktop-window`) and `Session`, the host for a component inside a view another application owns (flags `android-surface` or `desktop-window`). Still to come: the native Android host. It sits on top of the engine and passes the target flags down. See "The API" below.
- `packages/vessel/ui` (package `vessel-ui`): reusable components built on the API: `Container` (a component that holds and places children: `Container::new().with_display(Display::Flex).with_gap(8)`, also `with_direction`, `with_wrap`, `with_justify`, `with_align`, `with_columns`, `with_rows`; stacked by default), `Button` (event `Clicked`), `Label`, `Slider` (event `Changed(f32)`; optional `track_image` and `thumb_image` pictures replace the track and the round thumb, e.g. a color gradient for a color picker) and `Image` (a picture from pixels or a GPU frame, with `Fit`: Contain, Cover or Stretch). Each is a struct that holds a `Component` and implements only `Deref<Target = Component>` (that alone makes it `Renderable`, the trait everything shown, added to a parent or mounted must implement, so a type that cannot be drawn does not compile; `#[derive(Component)]` (from `vessel-macros`; it finds whichever vessel crate the caller depends on) writes the `Deref` and checks that its field is `Renderable` — the controls in `vessel-ui` all use it with `#[component(plain)]`, which skips the host-view `mount`/`unmount`/`Drop` that an app's own exported component gets). Their look follows reactive properties (`set_label`, `with_color`, ...), they use no abra and no platform code.
- `packages/vessel/gpu-passes`: the plain data that describes GPU work (`GpuPass`, `GpuAux`, `GpuSession`) and, with its `runtime` feature, the wgpu runtime that runs it.
- `packages/vessel/surface`: the surfaces that frames are drawn on, looked up by id (the `Surface` trait; a native Android window is the first kind).

Each app defines its own pieces in its own folder, not in the toolkit. The mobile app does it in `packages/react-native/alakazam` (its mini apps, its `Message` enum, and how a canvas is shown). The desktop app would do the same in `packages/node`.

## Engine

The engine "Vessel" is the core of the view system. It manages live views, handles messages, and decides when to draw frames on the surfaces.

## Surface

A surface is where the engine draws frames. This could be a react-native view, a window on the desktop, or any other platform-specific rendering target.

Surfaces live in `packages/vessel/surface`. `Surface` is a trait, so each kind of destination is added by implementing it and registering it under an id; the engine and the apps do not change. The platform's view registers its surface when it appears, resizes it, and destroys it when it goes away, and the renderer draws on whatever is registered under the id. Each kind is a cargo feature on the engine crate (`vessel`), off by default, so an app compiles only what it uses. The names say how the surface is owned, and the two groups can be combined:

- `*-surface`: inline component style, drawing inside a view that a host application owns.
- `*-window`: a standalone app or game, where Vessel owns the window and the main loop.

| Flag | What it gives you | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `android-surface` | An Android `Surface` handed over by any host UI (React Native, Flutter, a Java or Kotlin app) | Done, used by the mobile app |
| `desktop-window` | A native desktop window that Vessel opens and runs, bordered, borderless or fullscreen borderless. Keyboard and mouse arrive as `pub-sub` events. Drawn with the CPU | Done on Windows (winit and softbuffer) |
| `android-window` | A native Android app or game | Planned |
| `ios-surface`, `ios-window`, `web-surface` | The same pattern for other platforms | Not started |

A flag on a platform the build does not target compiles to nothing. A `*-window` flag reuses the platform's window kind from the matching `*-surface` (on Android both draw on an `ANativeWindow`; only who creates it differs).

An app usually starts with `use vessel::prelude::*;`. It brings in `Engine`, `View`, `Frame`, `MediaSource`, `Pacing` and `Waker`, the `pub-sub` types and traits (`subscribe` and `next` are trait methods, so they must be in scope), and the surface items for each flag that is on (for `desktop-window`: `desktop`, `WindowOptions`, `WindowFrame` and `DesktopEvent`). `vessel` also re-exports `pub_sub` and, with a flag on, `surface`.

To try the desktop window, run `cargo run -p vessel-window-test --bin vessel-window` (add `-- --borderless` or `-- --fullscreen`). Up and Down change the brightness and Escape closes it. The example uses no abra.

The platform entry points stay in the app, not in the crate. The mobile app's JNI functions are named after its Java package, so they live in `packages/react-native/alakazam` and call into the crate.

## The API

Status: the design is settled. The `vessel-api` crate exists with `Component`, `BehaviorSubject`, `Canvas`, neutral input and `run` for a desktop window; `App`, CSS-like layout (stack, flex, grid) and child regions are built; `Session` (a hosted component) is built; the native Android host is not. Layers, bottom to top: `pub-sub` (streams), `vessel` (the engine), `vessel-api` (what apps write), then reusable component crates such as a future `vessel-ui` (Button, Label, ...). Apps write `use vessel_api::prelude::*;`.

- **Everything is pub/sub.** The only verbs are `subscribe` and `next`. State is a `BehaviorSubject` or a `BehaviorSubject`, things that happen are a `Subject`. Operators (`map`, `filter_map`, `scan`, `merge`, `distinct_until_changed`, `combine_latest`, `take_until`) turn one stream into another. There is no `emit`, no string-named actions and no second event system.
- **Events live on components.** A `Component` is an `Observer<E>` for every event type `E` (`component.next(MyEvent::Clicked)` sends), and it has a pub-sub `Subject<E>` for each one (`component.subject::<MyEvent>().subscribe(|e| ...)` listens). There is no wrapper type: the accessors return the `pub_sub::Subject` itself. Named accessors: `keyboard()`, `pointer()`, `draw()`, `quit()`, and a control's own such as `button.subject::<Clicked>()` and `slider.subject::<Changed>()`. The app has no event bus. A parent hears a child only by subscribing on the child it holds (nothing bubbles automatically).
- **Components are reusable.** A definition (a function or a struct that builds a `Component`) can make any number of instances, each with its own state and subscriptions. Inputs are plain values with reactive setters; outputs are typed events. Layout (`.width(..)`, `.fill()`) is set on the instance by its parent.
- **Properties are reactive inside.** A component stores `BehaviorSubject<T>` values (a `BehaviorSubject` with `value()`/`set()` that ignores a set to an equal value, and `bind(&stream)` to follow a stream). Its draw code `watch`es the ones that change how it looks, so `button.set_label("Close")` redraws it and the user never creates a subject. Names follow the repo conventions: `with_*` builder, `set_*` setter, plain getter.
- **A component never knows its platform, and there is no separate context type.** A host (a desktop window, a native Android activity, a hosted React Native view, or a region of a parent) does exactly three things with the component it shows: it sets the component's `size()` property (and keeps it current as the window resizes), it sends the platform's input as neutral events (`component.next(KeyEvent { .. })`, `PointerEvent`), and it listens for `Quit` on the component to end the app. A component reads input with `component.subject::<KeyEvent>()` and `component.subject::<PointerEvent>()` (streams you can put operators on) and asks to quit with `component.next(Quit)`. `vessel_api::run(&component, AppOptions)` is the desktop host today (flag `desktop-window`); `desktop::run` in the surface crate is only its low-level API and apps do not call it. `Session::open(&component)` is the host for an inline component: `attach_surface(id)` (call again until true, since the host's view may appear later; the newest frame is kept and drawn on attach, and a component with no size takes the surface's), `resize(w, h)`, input by sending events to `session.component()`, and `close()`. Native Android will be another host of the same shape.
- **A window app can have child components.** A child gets a region of the parent's surface; its events are the parent's events filtered to the region and shifted into the child's coordinates; the parent computes layout. Children share the parent's engine. Keyboard goes to the focused component, pointer to the component under the cursor.

The dependency order is `pub-sub` < `vessel-engine` < `vessel-api` < `vessel-ui` < `vessel` (the umbrella); `gpu-passes` (feature `vessel-target`) sits on `vessel-engine`. The engine must never depend on the API or the controls. Apps (the mobile crate, the examples) depend on `vessel` only. Pictures made on the GPU go to the screen without a CPU copy: a source sends `GpuPicture` on `component.subject::<GpuPicture>()` (or `image.show_gpu(frame)`), a `GpuFrame` knows its GPU, so the `Session` asks the first one it shows for a `GpuTarget` (`target_for(surface_id)`) or reads it back (`read_back`) — the app never sets a target up; `gpu_passes::target::{TextureFrame, AndroidTarget}` are the wgpu implementations. The mobile photo is just a `vessel::Image` fed by the effect chain, and `packages/react-native/alakazam/src/live_view.rs` (the `LiveView` component React creates: an `Image` that follows the pictures, hosted by a vessel `Session`) is written like the panels example: the messages React sends are a `Subject`, the chain of effects is `messages.scan(..)` (plain data, a pure `Chain::after`), the picture is `chain.combine_latest(&direct).filter_map(render)`, and `image.set_source(&pictures)` is the only wiring (the `Image` keeps the stream alive; messages from the host arrive as the component's own `subject::<Message>()`; there is no GPU setup in the app; a source just sends a GPU picture when its GPU made one, and the engine draws or reads it back). The photo is a `LiveView` component the app defines itself (a struct that derefs to `Component`): apps make their own components; the toolkit does not grow for one app. No shared mutable state, no threads. Write new mini apps this way.

Build order (the first five are done): the `pub-sub` operators, then the API crate skeleton (`BehaviorSubject`, `Component` with typed events, `watch`, `draw`), then neutral input and `run` with the desktop host behind it, then `App`, layout and child regions, then `Session`, then the native Android host. The mobile editor's `LiveSession` (`packages/react-native/alakazam/src/session.rs`) now runs on `vessel_api::Session`: the main image is a `Component` that draws an abra canvas, listens for its own `Message` events (`component.subject::<Message>().subscribe`) and redraws by bumping a `BehaviorSubject` revision that its `draw` listener reads. `Session::drawn()` (a `Subject<Drawn>`) lets the host time message-to-pixels.

Children and layout: there is one kind of component and any component can hold children, like an element in HTML. How it places them is a setting on it, like CSS: `Component::new("page").with_display(Display::Flex).with_direction(Direction::Column).with_gap(8).with_padding(8)`. `Display` is `Stack` (the default, children on top of each other), `Flex` (a line, `Row` by default, with `wrap`, `gap`, `padding`, `justify`, `align`) or `Grid` (`with_columns([Track::Px(200), Track::Fr(1.0)])`, `with_rows`). Each setting has a `with_*` that chains and a `set_*` that changes it later and redraws. A child says what it wants with `.width(px)`, `.height(px)`, `.fill()` (the default), `.grow(share)` and `.span(columns, rows)`. There are no `Row`, `Column` or `Stack` types and none should be added. Flex and grid are our own code in `layout.rs` (no layout dependency; `taffy` was tried and removed on purpose), and follow the CSS rules closely enough to be familiar. The app is `App::new(title).add(page).run()`. The first child added has the keyboard, a click gives it to the child under the pointer, and `child.focus()` sets it by hand. Keys go only to the focused child; pointer events go to the child under the cursor (or the one that was pressed, until release) with coordinates shifted into the child. Nothing bubbles except `Quit`, which reaches the host. A component that owns a listener on itself uses `component.keep(subscription)` and refers to itself with `component.downgrade()` (a `WeakComponent`), so there is no reference cycle. Only children that changed are redrawn, and `Canvas::draw_pixels` blends them into the parent. Fonts are inherited like CSS, and the size and the typeface inherit separately: `component.set_font_size(24)` and `set_font_face(Face)` style all text inside it, a child's own setting overrides just that part, and `inherit_font()` goes back. Where nothing in the app sets one, the host supplies the default with `component.set_default_font(Font)`: `run` (a window app) gives the system's interface font (`Face::system()`, found at the usual file paths for Windows, Android, macOS and Linux, with the built-in bitmap as the last resort), while `Session::set_default_font` is for the application that owns the view, which passes its own font (a session never guesses, so until it does text uses the built-in bitmap). A `draw()` listener reads the result as `canvas.font()`; `draw_text` and `text_size` use it. Outline faces are drawn with the `fontdue` crate (TrueType and OpenType files via `Face::from_file` or `Face::from_bytes`); there is no kerning, shaping or bold/italic yet. Theme works the same way as fonts, like CSS custom properties: `Theme` is the full set of values (`background`, `surface`, `text`, `muted_text`, `control`, `border`, `accent`, `accent_text`, `track`, `radius`), `ThemePatch` sets some of them, and each value inherits on its own. The host supplies the default with `set_default_theme` (`run` gives `Theme::system()`: the user's dark or light setting and accent color, read from the Windows registry through `surface::desktop::appearance()`; other platforms are light until their reading is written; `Session::set_default_theme` is for the app that owns the view, which knows its own look). Any component restyles what is inside it with `set_theme(Theme::dark())` or `set_theme(ThemePatch::new().accent(..))`, and `inherit_theme()` goes back. Ui components take their look from the theme and only an explicit `set_color`, `set_radius` and so on overrides one thing; a `draw()` listener reads `canvas.theme()`. `with_background(Background::Page | Surface | Color(..))` fills a component's area from the theme (not inherited, like CSS `background`), and `App`'s root uses `Page`. **Every event in these crates is a stream** (input `keyboard()`/`pointer()`, drawing `draw()`, `button.subject::<Clicked>()`, `slider.subject::<Changed>()`, `component.subject::<E>()`); the only verbs are `subscribe` and `next`. Drawing is one of them: `gradient.subject::<Canvas>().subscribe(|canvas| ..)` (asking for `draw()` also asks for a redraw), where the `Canvas` is a cheap shared handle (its methods take `&self`) so several listeners can draw on the same one. Never add a callback setter such as `draw(closure)`, an `on(..)`, an `emit`, or an API that makes the caller hold a `Subscription`: `stream.subscribe(handler)` is plain pub-sub: a component's streams are `Subject::persistent()`, whose listeners last as long as the subject (so they go with the component) and whose returned `Subscription` can simply be dropped (only `subscription.unsubscribe()` stops one early). The handler's argument type is inferred from the stream (no `: &Type` annotations). Ordinary `Subject::new()` streams and operator results keep drop-to-stop. Everything is automatic; app code declares as little as possible. A component's `draw()` listeners depend on whatever properties they read: `BehaviorSubject::value()` (so `BehaviorSubject::value()` and the value of a `scan`) reports each read to a thread-local tracker (`pub_sub::tracking`), the component listens for those values, and it redraws when one changes (and forgets values a later draw no longer reads). So there is no `.watch(..)` in app or ui code; `watch` is only for a source whose value `draw` does not read. State is derived, not stored: `let on = button.subject::<Clicked>().scan(false, |on, _| !*on)` flips on each click, `component.subject::<E>()` is the typed stream of any event, and a control's own value (`slider.value()`) can be read straight from another component's `draw`. An app quits on a key with `App::with_quit_key("Escape")`, and global shortcuts are `app.root().subject::<KeyEvent>().subscribe(|key| ..)` (the root hears every key, so no focus is needed). If code you write makes a user do bookkeeping the framework could do, fix the framework instead. Listening is just `stream.subscribe(handler)` on a component's stream: the persistent subject keeps the listener until the component is dropped, so nobody holds a `Subscription` and there is no `keep(..)` clutter in app code. Because `subscribe` returns a `Subscription`, not the component, build the component in a `let` first and then `component.subject::<Canvas>().subscribe(..)`. The handler must not capture a strong clone of that same component (use `downgrade()`). A stream made by an operator (`component.subject::<KeyEvent>().filter_map(..)`) is an ordinary stream whose `subscribe` gives a `Subscription` to hold (or `keep`). Every component has the same CSS-like box, set with `with_*` / `set_*` pairs: `padding` and `margin` (`Edges`: a number, `[up_down, left_right]` or `[top, right, bottom, left]`), `border_width` and `border_color`, `radius` (pixels or `Radius::Theme`) and `background` (`Background::Color/Page/Surface/Control/Accent`), plus the child sizes `width`, `height`, `fill`, `grow`, `span`. Sizes are border-box (padding and border are inside a fixed size). A parent's layout keeps a child's margin clear and gives the child the rectangle inside it; for flex, spare room is shared first and margins are added to each child's share. The framework draws the box (background following the radius, then the component's `draw`, then children, then the border on top), so a component's `draw()` listeners only draw its content: it reads `canvas.content_rect()` (inside border and padding) and `canvas.radius()` to follow its own shape. Do not draw backgrounds or borders in a ui component's `draw()` listener; give it the box defaults instead (`Button` is `Background::Control`, border 1, `Radius::Theme`). Because `with_*` on the `Component` returns a `Component`, call a control's own `with_*` first when chaining. Slider does not honor padding yet. Not built: per-side border, border style, min/max size, opacity, overflow clipping. Inheritance follows CSS: font (size and typeface), theme values (like custom properties, `accent-color` and `color-scheme`) and text color inherit down the tree; background, border, radius-of-a-component, padding, gap, direction and the other layout settings do not. Form controls are the CSS exception: like a browser's `<button>`, a `Button` does not take its parents' font (`set_inherits_font(false)` is set by the control; call `set_inherits_font(true)` for CSS `font: inherit`) and uses the theme's `control_text`, not the page's `text`. Follow this for every new control. Never hard-code colors in a ui component. A default `Button` must look like the platform's plain control (light gray face, thin gray border, small radius, ordinary text, as in a browser); the accent-filled look is opt-in with `with_primary(true)`. Drawing: `Canvas` has `fill_rounded_rect` (radius 0 is square, half the size is a circle), `stroke_rounded_rect`, `draw_text` and `text_size` (the built-in 8x8 ASCII bitmap face from the `font8x8` crate, or an outline face; real font rendering is still to do), all blended by alpha with smoothed edges. Not built yet: min and max sizes, `align_self`, and content-sized (auto) tracks, because components have no intrinsic size. `apps/examples/vessel-panels` shows a reusable `Button` used twice in a flex column beside a gradient (`cargo run -p vessel-panels-test --bin vessel-panels`).


## Events

The engine is an event driven system. It uses a pub/sub mechanism to communicate changes and updates between different parts of the system.

Using `target.next()` allows you to trigger an event to the system, notifying all subscribers of the change.

The system then watches for these events and updates the relevant parts of the engine accordingly.

## GPU Passes

GPU passes represent the work that needs to be done on the GPU. They are described as plain data structures and executed by the GPU runtime. This separation allows the engine to manage and schedule GPU work efficiently without being tied to a specific GPU implementation.

# Rules

- Nothing under `packages/vessel` may depend on abra. If a piece needs abra types, it belongs in the app's folder or in a small adapter, not in the toolkit.
- Design with this question: "how can X hook into gpu, live or events?" The toolkit defines the places to plug in, and other code plugs into them. For example, abra gives the GPU crate the passes it needs as data; abra does not run the GPU itself.
- The app sends only what changed (a message with the new value), never its whole state. The engine decides when to draw. A mini app changes its own state and never says "draw".
- Do not hard-code crate names in docs or code that you can avoid. They may be renamed before publishing.
- Packaging is the host's job. A `*-surface` flag (React Native or any host app) needs no packaging tool from Vessel: the host's own build (Gradle for React Native) makes the APK and loads our library. Only a `*-window` build where Vessel owns the whole app on a platform with no build of its own (a standalone native Android app) needs one, such as `cargo-apk`, and then it is a command a developer runs, never a dependency of the crates.

## Hosts and bindings

The core (`pub-sub`, `vessel-engine`, `vessel-api`, `vessel-ui`) knows no platform. A host gives it a surface and input; a binding lets another UI system mount a component. Android: the `surface` crate (feature `android-surface`) exports the JNI natives of the Java class `dev.vessel.android.SurfaceBridge`; `packages/react-native/vessel` (`@vessel/react-native`) holds that Java class, a `TextureView` host (`VesselTextureView`), the React Native `VesselViewManager`/`VesselPackage` (autolinked) and the `<VesselView surfaceId=.../>` component. An app writes no Java and no JNI: it names its native library once in its own app manifest (inside `<application>`; a library manifest is regenerated by ubrn and would lose it) (`<meta-data android:name="dev.vessel.library" android:value="..."/>`) and uses `VesselView`. Planned: the engine owns sessions and attaching (the app passes a component handle to the view instead of a surface id), touch input, and the system font/theme.

## Showing a component on a host's view

`vessel::mount(view, &component)` puts a component on a host view by number; the engine opens the session when that view's surface appears (in either order, and again if the surface comes back) and `vessel::unmount` takes it off. An app never opens a `Session`, attaches a surface or retries. `Image::track(&source)` makes an `Image` follow anything that implements `Trackable` (`pictures(size)`, the size being the view's); derived pub-sub streams of a persistent subject (`component.subject::<E>()`) are persistent too, so `messages.filter(..).subscribe(..)` needs nothing held. The mobile `LiveView` (`packages/react-native/alakazam/src/live_view.rs`) is just that: `Image::new().track(&abra_image)`, a `Message::{SliderMove(value, key), Action(key)}` subject, and `#[derive(uniffi::Object, Component)]` (the `Component` derive is in `packages/vessel/macros`, re-exported by `vessel`; it uses the field marked `#[component]` or else the first), which generates the exported `mount`/`unmount` that a `<VesselView source={liveView}/>` calls (it picks its own view number) and takes the component off its views when dropped, so the app writes no mounting code; `live_effects.rs` says what each key shows, and `AbraImage` implements `Trackable` (it redraws after every edit and shows the live effects over its pixels).

Touch: the Android `VesselTextureView` sends each touch to `SurfaceBridge.nativeTouch`; the `surface` crate publishes it as `SurfaceEvent::Touched`, and `vessel::mount`'s listener hands it to the component mounted on that view as `PointerEvent::Moved` plus a `Button` down/up, in the view's own pixels. So a vessel `Slider` (or any component listening to `subject::<PointerEvent>()`) works on the phone with no app code. The mobile `SkinTanColorPicker` is a `Slider` with a gradient `track_image` and a `thumb_image`, whose `Changed` values go to the `ImagePreview` as `Message::SliderMove("action-skin-tan", value)`; the tan scale (`skin_tan_gradient()` in `effect_spec.rs`) draws the bar and gives `EffectSpec::SkinTan` its color.
